transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Korova Coleman.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says a passenger jet going from Dubai to Tel Aviv
made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia today.
One of the pilots reportedly stabbed the other pilot and then tried to crash the plane.
NPR's Eya Batrawi reports.
Netanyahu says the plane went into a spin and began to plunge as one of the pilots was
trying to sabotage the aircraft's systems after stabbing his co-pilot.
He says nearly all passengers on board were Israeli and that the plane landed safely at
Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
Netanyahu says the suspected attacker is being questioned now by Saudi authorities, though
Saudi Arabia has yet to confirm that.
Fly Dubai says the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia after a
"altercation occurred" in the flight deck.
The airline deployed two replacement aircraft to bring the passengers from Tabuk to Tel
Aviv and cautioned that the motives behind the incident are unknown and remain subject
to a formal investigation.
Israel's defense minister, however, called it an attempted jihadist terrorist attack
but provided no further details.
Eya Batrawi, NPR News, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
Officials at Cornell University are facing growing criticism over their handling of an
alleged rape case in 2024.
NPR's Brian Mann reports New York Governor Kathy Hochul is calling for an independent
investigation.
Hochul called a woman's account of being drugged and gang-raped at Cornell in 2024 horrifying.
She says there are serious questions and is calling for a transparent, independent review
of the university's response.
A local prosecutor says the alleged victim described parts of the incident as consensual
at the time, but potential evidence of violence by seven male students was only investigated
by campus police, not by city police.
Ithaca's Mayor Robert Cantelmo has also blasted Cornell's response.
In a statement to NPR, Cornell University says it will work with elected officials to
address safety concerns.
They didn't say whether they will approve an independent investigation.
Ryan Mann, NPR News, Ithaca, New York.
A FEMA-backed program is running out of money.
It's helped hundreds of survivors of last year's Los Angeles fires navigate the rebuilding
process.
NPR's Kirk Siegler has more.
As is typical after bad wildfires, last year FEMA approved $13 million toward its disaster
case management program, which pairs a case manager to fire survivors like Sophia Vidal,
helping them with insurance, securing building permits, and a grant so that her husband,
who's a contractor, could replace his tools that burned in the fire.
We need her guidance to help us get back on track as far as what we need to do next.
David Vidal and some 1,300 other survivors are now losing their case managers, as only
3 million of the promise, 13 million in aid, has actually been distributed in the L.A.
burn zones.
Kirk Siegler, NPR News, Los Angeles.
You're listening to NPR News.
The Pentagon says the U.S. military has formally left Iraq.
In a statement, the Defense Department says the U.S. has concluded its military mission
there.
It also says Iraq now has the primary responsibility for addressing its own military challenges.
As Pennsylvania and other states continue to deal with a large measles outbreak, other
states are alerting the public about possible exposures to the highly contagious virus.
NPR's Rachel Carson reports on what travelers should know.
An exposure happens when a person comes into contact with someone who has measles.
Like in California, when an infected, unvaccinated passenger traveled throughout the state on
trains and buses.
Up to 9 out of 10 people exposed to measles could get sick, if they're not protected.
Dr. Paul Offit is the director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital
of Philadelphia.
You don't have to come in direct contact with someone who has measles to get infected.
You just have to be within their airspace, within two hours of them being there.
Offit says protection, in this case, means being fully vaccinated, with two doses of
the MMR vaccine.
That not only helps protect you, but people who can't be or aren't yet vaccinated, like
those with compromised immune systems or infants.
Rachel Carlson, NPR News.
A government report on inflation that's watched by the Federal Reserve says inflation rose
a little less than expected last month.
This report says inflation is running at an annual rate of 3.4 percent.
That's compared to 3.7 percent a year ago at this time.
This is NPR.
This election season, you can streamline your news intake with Up First.
Our team of reporters and editors works overnight, so you can start every morning with three
stories you need to know.
In short episodes, 12-14 minutes long to save you time and your sanity.
Follow up first on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

topics.text: Pilot stabs co-pilot on Dubai to Tel Aviv flight, plane makes emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
Cornell University faces criticism over handling of alleged 2024 rape case, Governor Hochul calls for investigation
FEMA disaster case management program runs out of money for Los Angeles fire survivors
Pentagon announces U.S. military has formally concluded its mission and left Iraq
Measles outbreak spreads across multiple states including Pennsylvania and California among unvaccinated travelers
Government inflation report shows annual rate of 3.4 percent, lower than previous year's 3.7 percent
